- When sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.75) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5% relative to historical mean or recent peak.
- When sentiment is bearish (≤0.25) and prices are trending down, model often underestimates the drop; adjust downward by 3–8% to match observed mean reversion.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days), model frequently overshoots in next 5–10 days; apply a “cool-down” correction: subtract 1–3% per day post-spike.
- If sentiment is mixed (0.25–0.75) and price is near recent 10-day average, model often drifts away; anchor forecast to 10-day moving average or use sentiment-weighted median.
- For 30-day forecasts, model consistently underestimates true price volatility in bearish sentiment periods; increase forecast variance by 10–20% if sentiment <0.3.
- When sentiment is high and price is near support level, model often fails to recognize reversal; add a 1–3% downward bias to prevent overconfidence in continuation.
- If sentiment is low and price is near resistance, model tends to ignore support; apply a 2–5% downward adjustment to avoid overestimating breakout potential.
